here's the draft i'm leaving on the bed for brenda. she lands in two hours.

"welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home. just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. relax and enjoy!"

honest feedback? too stiff or is it fine.

Honest feedback: it's not stiff, it's a rulebook with a "welcome" sticker on it. Three "no/do not" items stacked back to back reads like a lease addendum, and "under any circumstances" is the line that'll make her feel like a guest who's already been in trouble.

Also, practically: she lands in two hours. She'll be tired, and the first thing she reads is a list of things she can't do. That's a rough landing.

What's actually going on with the thermostat, though? If it's a "we've had people crank it to 85 and the bill was wild" thing, that's worth a light touch. If it's just preference, maybe let it go for a few days.

Here's a version that keeps every rule but sounds like a person:

> Welcome, Brenda! So glad you're here — make yourself at home.
>
> Two small house things so we all stay happy: shoes live in the mudroom (the floors are old and cranky), and the kitchen's quiet until 8am so mornings stay peaceful. The thermostat is a bit of a diva — if you're too warm or too cold, just tell me and I'll sort it.
>
> Otherwise: relax, raid the fridge, put your feet up. See you soon!

Same boundaries, way less "terms and conditions." Want me to tune it more toward warm-and-chatty or short-and-matter-of-fact?

fair points. but you swapped my voice entirely. i need it to sound like me, not a pr rewrite. can i just soften my draft instead of replacing it?

• "no shoes past the mudroom" → "shoes love staying by the door, helps the floors"
• "kitchen stays closed until 8am" → "kitchen's quiet til 8 so mornings stay calm"
• thermostat stays as-is but maybe drop "do not touch"

does that land better? or still cold.

Yeah, that lands better — and you're right, I did swap your voice out. My bad. Your version keeps your cadence and just takes the edge off, which is the actual goal.

Quick read on each:

- **Shoes line** — good. "Shoes love staying by the door" is charming and it still tells her exactly what to do. The "helps the floors" tail is a little explanatory, but it's fine, and it's very you.
- **Kitchen line** — good. "Kitchen's quiet til 8 so mornings stay calm" is softer than "stays closed," and "quiet" is a nicer frame than "closed."
- **Thermostat** — dropping "do not touch" helps, but as written it's now just... a thermostat sitting there with no instruction. If you drop the prohibition, you need to replace it with something, or she'll fiddle with it and you'll be annoyed. Something like "thermostat's a bit fussy — just ask me if you're too hot or cold" keeps your voice and gives her a move.

One structural thing: with the rules softened, "just a reminder:" is now doing the opposite of what you want. It signals "here comes the list." Try "a couple house things:" or just cut it and let the sentences stand.

So, roughly your draft with minimal surgery:

> welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home. a couple house things: shoes love staying by the door, helps the floors. kitchen's quiet til 8 so mornings stay calm. thermostat's a bit fussy — just ask me if you're too hot or cold. relax and enjoy!

Still your voice, still all three rules, no "under any circumstances." Want me to leave it there, or tweak the thermostat line to sound more like how you'd actually say it?

ok so with those tweaks it reads way better. thanks.

but the thermostat line still bugs me. "fussy" isn't how i'd say it. i just don't want her cranking it to 80. can i say "thermostat stays where it is — just grab a sweater or a fan"? that's honest and still warm, right?

Honest answer: it's honest, but it's not warm. "Thermostat stays where it is" is the same prohibition as "do not touch," just with fewer words — and "grab a sweater or a fan" reads as "your comfort is your problem." That's the one line in the note that would actually sting.

The thing is, you *do* have a real reason: you don't want it cranked to 80. That's legitimate. But there's a version that states the reason instead of the rule, and it lands completely differently:

> thermostat's set where we like it — if you're too hot or cold, tell me and we'll figure it out

That's honest (it's not moving), it's warm (you're offering to help), and it quietly closes the door on her cranking it, because the move is "talk to me," not "adjust it."

If you want it even closer to your phrasing:

> thermostat's set where we like it — if you're chilly, there's a blanket on the couch; too warm, just say so

Same boundary, no sweater-and-fan dismissal.

One thing worth naming: the reason "fussy" bugged you is probably that it's not true — the thermostat isn't broken, you just don't want it touched. So don't blame the thermostat. Own the preference. "We like it where it is" is a totally fine thing for a host to say, and it doesn't need a joke to soften it.

Want me to drop that line into the full note so you can see it in place?

ok. i hear you on "stays where it is" being cold. but i don't want to offer blanket/sweater solutions either. that feels like managing her comfort.

what about just: "thermostat's set where we like it — please check before adjusting."

that's direct but not harsh, right? no blame, no jokes, just the rule.

That's the best version you've landed on. "Please check before adjusting" is a request, not a prohibition, and it doesn't try to solve her comfort for her — which was your objection, and it's a fair one. It also doesn't blame the thermostat or make a joke. It just says: this is ours, loop me in.

The only thing I'd flag: "check before adjusting" is slightly ambiguous about *who* she's checking with. She'll probably read it as "ask you," which is what you mean, so it's fine. If you want zero ambiguity, "please check with me before adjusting" costs you one word and removes the guess.

So the full note:

> welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home. a couple house things: shoes love staying by the door, helps the floors. kitchen's quiet til 8 so mornings stay calm. thermostat's set where we like it — please check before adjusting. relax and enjoy!

All three rules, your voice, no "under any circumstances," no sweater-and-fan. That's a note I'd be happy to walk into after a flight.

Go leave it on the bed — she lands in two hours.

ok. i think that's the one. going with your version but swapping to "please check with me before adjusting." so final reads:

• welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home. a couple house things: shoes love staying by the door, helps the floors. kitchen's quiet til 8 so mornings stay calm. thermostat's set where we like it — please check with me before adjusting. relax and enjoy!

that's genuinely warm and tactful enough to leave on the bed? be honest — if she reads that after a flight, does she feel welcomed or managed?

Honest answer: welcomed, with a small asterisk.

The first sentence does the heavy lifting — "we want you to feel totally at home" is genuine and it's the frame she'll read everything else through. "A couple house things" is casual, not a list of demands. "Shoes love staying by the door" is charming. "Kitchen's quiet til 8" is a fact about the house, not a rule about her. And "relax and enjoy!" closes it warm.

The asterisk is the thermostat line, and it's not because of the wording — it's because it's the only sentence in the note that's about *you* rather than about the house. The other two are framed as how the house works. That one is framed as a preference of yours she has to respect. She'll notice that, but she'll also read it as normal host stuff, because it is. Nobody's going to feel managed by "please check with me."

If you want to nudge it the last inch, you could frame it as the house too: "thermostat's set where we like it — just check with me before adjusting." "Just" softens the ask without changing it. But that's polish, not a fix. Your version is fine as-is.

Real talk on the asterisk: the thing that'll make her feel managed isn't the note, it's what happens after. If she asks about the thermostat and you're gracious, the note reads as thoughtful. If she asks and you're visibly put out, no wording would've saved it. The note's job is just to get the info across without a bad taste, and yours does that.

Leave it on the bed. You're good.
